article.title: Why Waiting Time Explodes Near Full Capacity
article.why: 用 queueing intuition 理解利用率接近滿載時等待時間為何非線性上升，以及 slack 為何是可靠性資源。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
A service system can look efficient when almost every worker, machine, or server is busy. Yet the same system may feel terrible to customers because waiting time rises sharply as utilization approaches full capacity. This is one of the most important ideas in queueing theory: a small increase in utilization near the limit can create a much larger increase in delay.

Consider a simple checkout with one cashier. If customers arrive at perfectly regular intervals and every transaction takes exactly the same time, the cashier could theoretically operate close to 100% utilization without a long line. Real systems are not that smooth. Customers arrive in bursts, transaction times vary, questions occur, payments fail, and employees occasionally need a break. Variability creates moments when demand temporarily exceeds available capacity.

When utilization is low, the system has room to absorb those bursts. If the cashier is busy only half the time, a short rush may create a line, but the queue can disappear during the next quiet period. At 95% utilization, quiet periods are rare. Each burst adds work faster than the system can remove it, so unfinished demand carries into the next burst.

This is why “unused capacity” is not always waste. Spare capacity acts as a buffer against uncertainty. Hospitals need some beds and staff that are not continuously occupied. Cloud platforms need headroom for traffic spikes. Call centers schedule more agents than the exact average workload would require. Manufacturing lines often need slack around bottlenecks. The purpose is not to maximize idle time; it is to prevent normal variation from turning into persistent congestion.

A useful intuition comes from the relationship among arrival rate, service rate, and utilization. If demand grows toward the maximum service rate, the margin between what arrives and what can be processed becomes very small. The system then needs increasingly long quiet periods to recover from random peaks. Because those quiet periods occur less often, waiting can grow nonlinearly rather than in a neat straight line.

Managers sometimes respond to this problem by asking employees to work faster. That may help temporarily, but it can also increase error rates, rework, or burnout. Another response is to reduce variability: standardize requests, improve scheduling, separate simple cases from complex ones, or remove avoidable handoffs. A third response is to add capacity at the true bottleneck rather than everywhere.

The location of the bottleneck matters. Adding five people to an upstream team does little if every case must still pass through one overloaded reviewer. In fact, extra upstream capacity can make the queue in front of the reviewer even larger. Capacity decisions should therefore follow the flow of work, not just local utilization percentages.

Priority rules also change waiting. An emergency department may deliberately allow routine cases to wait so critical cases can be treated first. A software team may reserve capacity for incidents. These systems are not optimizing one average waiting time; they are balancing different service objectives and risk levels.

There is also a measurement trap. If managers reward teams mainly for high utilization, local teams have an incentive to keep themselves busy even when the overall process would benefit from slack. A reviewer may build a large queue to guarantee that there is always work available. The reviewer looks productive, but customers experience longer cycle time.

The better operating question is not “How close can we get to 100%?” It is “How much capacity margin do we need for the variability and service level we face?” The answer depends on arrival patterns, service-time variation, customer tolerance, and the cost of delay. In some systems, 90% utilization is acceptable. In others, even 80% can create unacceptable queues.

The strategic lesson is that capacity is not only a cost item. It is also a reliability resource. Near full utilization, the value of the next unit of spare capacity can be much greater than the value of the previous one because it restores the system's ability to recover from ordinary randomness. That is why well-designed operations often look slightly underused when viewed at a single moment but perform much better over time.

quiz.question: Why does a system recover easily at low utilization?
quiz.answer: Because quiet periods provide spare capacity to clear temporary queues.

quiz.question: Why can adding upstream staff make a bottleneck worse?
quiz.answer: It can send work faster into an already overloaded downstream stage.

quiz.question: Output: Explain why 100% utilization can be risky in one sentence.
quiz.answer: Example: Near 100% utilization, normal variability has no spare capacity to absorb it, so queues grow quickly.
